note: Published relative risks (RR) used as PRIORS when no observed city data has been fitted. beta_a = ln(RR) / a_ref, where a_ref is the model's anomaly driver at the published exposure. These are order-of-magnitude anchors, not fits. Edit or add entries, then run: python backend/calibrate_risk.py --anchors-only

anchors.source: de Bont et al. 2024, Environment International 184:108461 (PMC11790314) - Ahmedabad: +24.9% (95% CI 21.7 to 28.2) daily all-cause deaths on heatwave days, defined as daily mean temperature above the city's 97th percentile for 2 consecutive days, 2008-2019 municipal death registers
anchors.caveat: The study's exposure is daily MEAN temperature above the 97th percentile; TAPAS's anomaly driver is a Tmax departure from the ERA5 normal. a_ref = 0.5 (IMD Heat Wave onset) equates the two by assumption. A 97th-percentile mean-temperature event is probably milder than a 4.5 C Tmax departure, so this probably understates the slope.

anchors.source: de Bont et al. 2024, Environment International 184:108461 (PMC11790314) - Mumbai: +3.4% (95% CI 0.8 to 6.1), same definition and study as above; the paper reports Mumbai among the weakest associations of the ten cities
anchors.caveat: Same exposure mapping and a_ref = 0.5 assumption as the Ahmedabad entry. The small effect is a published finding for Mumbai, not a modelling choice.

anchors.source: de Bont et al. 2024, Environment International 184:108461 (PMC11790314) - pooled across ten Indian cities: +14.7% (95% CI 10.3 to 19.3), same definition
anchors.caveat: Pooled value, not city-specific: Chennai's and Hyderabad's own estimates are in the paper's supplementary Table S1, which was not read. Replace with the city values when entered. Same a_ref = 0.5 assumption. Hyderabad's registry covers only 2008 to June 2011 in this study.

anchors.source: Azhar et al. 2014, PLOS ONE 9(3):e91831 - mortality rate ratio in the peak heat week (19-25 May 2010); the paper gives 1.76 and 2.12 depending on the reference period
anchors.reason: Kept for reference, not used. It is a single extreme episode under a different exposure definition, so using it next to the de Bont estimates for other cities would make Ahmedabad look about twice as sensitive as the same method gives.

anchors.source: de Bont et al. 2024 - pooled +33.2% (95% CI 18.6 to 49.8) for mean temperature above the 99th percentile for at least 5 consecutive days; only occurred in 6 of the 10 cities (not Mumbai)
anchors.reason: Kept for reference, not used. A stricter definition than the one applied to the other cities; switching it on would give inconsistent cities.

anchors.source: Summer temperature and all-cause mortality 2006-2015, Hyderabad (PMC8843295) - about +16% mean daily deaths at Tmax >= 40 C
anchors.reason: Exposure is an absolute temperature threshold, not a departure from the city's normal, so it cannot be mapped onto the model's anomaly scale from this data alone.

not_calibrated.hosp: No published heat-admissions RR for these Indian cities was found that maps onto this model (a neonatal-ICU study in one Ahmedabad hospital and European studies do not represent city-wide admissions). Hospitalization stays on the default until admissions data is added to observed.csv.

Ahmedabad.note: mean daily all-cause deaths, 2008 to June 2019 (de Bont et al. 2024, Table 1); population has grown since

Chennai.note: mean daily all-cause deaths, 2010 to 2019 (de Bont et al. 2024, Table 1)

Hyderabad.note: mean daily all-cause deaths, 2008 to June 2011 (de Bont et al. 2024, Table 1); population has grown since

Mumbai.note: mean daily all-cause deaths, 2009 to Nov 2015 (de Bont et al. 2024, Table 1); population has grown since
